the two ways owners earn: price appreciation (share price rises) and dividends (company distributes part of its earnings)
common stock vs preferred stock: voting ownership vs fixed-priority shares (preferred dividends paid first; preferred stands ahead of common in liquidation)
why companies issue stock: raising money without borrowing (pay off debt, launch products, expand, enlarge facilities)
what shareholders get: a claim on the company's fortunes, with voting rights in common stock
the risks: prices fall as well as rise; no guarantee of gains; common stockholders last in line in bankruptcy

common-stock dividends are variable (may increase, decrease, or stop); preferred dividends are typically set/constant
large-company stocks as a group have lost money on average about one out of every three years (SEC)
a stock's price reflects market expectations (e.g., the P/E ratio as a measure of market expectations)

claims.claim: A share of stock signifies an ownership position — called equity — in a corporation and a claim on its proportional share of the corporation's assets and profits; stocks are also called equities, and most stocks carry voting rights such as electing corporate directors.

Investors buy stocks for three reasons: capital appreciation (a rise in the stock's price), dividend payments (the company distributes some of its earnings to stockholders), and the ability to vote shares and influence the company.

There are two main kinds of stock: common stock entitles owners to vote at shareholder meetings and receive dividends (after preferred holders); preferred stockholders usually do not have voting rights but receive dividends before common stockholders and have priority over them if the company goes bankrupt and its assets are liquidated.

Companies issue stock to raise money for purposes including paying off debt, launching new products, expanding into new markets or regions, and enlarging facilities; the first time a company sells stock to the public is an initial public offering (IPO).

Stock prices move down as well as up; there is no guarantee that the company whose stock you hold will grow and do well, so investors can lose money; large-company stocks as a group have lost money on average about one out of every three years.
In a bankruptcy liquidation, bondholders are paid first, then preferred stockholders, then common stockholders, who get whatever is left — which may be nothing.
Common-stock dividends are variable and may increase or decrease, while preferred stock typically carries a set (constant) dividend that the company is obligated to pay before any common dividend.

A stock's price reflects the market's expectations about the company: valuation ratios such as the price-to-earnings ratio 'show the expectations of the market' and represent the price an investor pays per unit of current or future earnings — the basis for the framing that a stock is a claim on a story that is still being written.

A company is considered public when its securities trade on public markets and it discloses certain business and financial information regularly to the public; private companies have no such public reporting obligations.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether stock ownership guarantees any return over time.
positions: SEC Investor.gov: stock prices move down as well as up; there is no guarantee the company will grow and do well; investors can lose money.

SEC Investor.gov also notes that investors willing to stick with stocks over long periods, say 15 years, generally have been rewarded with strong positive returns — a general historical observation, not a guarantee.
CFI: if the business does poorly the value of the share declines and the investor may lose some or all of the investment.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches both ways to earn and the honest risk note (prices fall as well as rise, no guarantee, common stockholders last in line in liquidation) and makes no predictive or advice claims about future returns.

positions: SEC Investor.gov lists dividends among the reasons investors buy stocks, framing them as distributions of some of the company's earnings.

OpenStax Principles of Finance 11.4: common-stock dividends are variable and may increase or decrease, and are paid only after preferred dividends; preferred dividends are typically set at a constant amount.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states that dividends are decided by the company, are not guaranteed, and vary for common stock, with preferred dividends paid first.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Finance, Section 11.1: Multiple Approaches to Stock Valuation
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook). Fetched live, HTTP 200, on 2026-08-21 (openstax.org serves full page content in the initial HTML). Supports: the P/E ratio as one of the most consistently used calculations in common-stock evaluation, computed as price per share divided by earnings per share; the P/E ratio as representative of the price an investor must pay for every unit of current (or future) corporate earnings and as showing the expectations of the market — the basis for the lesson's honest framing that a stock's price is a market guess about the company's future. Footer restricts AI ingestion; concepts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Finance, Section 11.4: Preferred Stock
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook). Fetched live, HTTP 200, on 2026-08-21. Supports: preferred stock as a form of equity offering preferential claims in ownership; a preferred dividend the company is obligated to pay before any dividend to common stockholders; priority claim to assets over common stockholders in bankruptcy and liquidation; preferred stockholders usually entitled to a set (constant) dividend every period; preferred stock has no maturity date (unlike bonds); cumulative vs noncumulative preferred features; Table 11.7 differences: common dividends paid only after preferred and variable, preferred dividends highest priority and constant. Footer restricts AI ingestion; facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: What are Stocks, Bonds, and Mutual Funds?
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B (reputable secondary). Fetched live, HTTP 200, on 2026-08-21. Supports: when an investor buys a stock, part ownership in the form of a share is bought; if the business does well the investor benefits from an increase in the value of the share; if it does poorly the value declines and the investor may lose some or all of the investment; companies sell stock to develop new products, expand into new markets, or pay off debt; the first sale of stock is an initial public offering (IPO); stocks as riskier than bonds with no guarantee, while bonds are a loan repaid with interest and are paid before shareholders in bankruptcy.
